clue.text: Messed about, like Hogwarts Harry?

blocks.note: first meaning: ... about, idled aimlessly
second, whimsical meaning: made into Harry Potter, the boy wizard of Hogwarts school

explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning is a playful coinage: to be 'Pottered' is to resemble Harry Potter. The question mark flags the invented sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To potter is to busy oneself in a relaxed, unproductive way, which is messing about; the pun turns the wizard's surname into a verb.

clue.text: Single, very depressed we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is a sound, so the phrase before is judged by how it is spoken

blocks.note: very = so, depressed = low; spoken together they make a word for one performer

explanation.surface: A lonely single person is feeling very down.
explanation.definitionFit: A solo performance or flight is done by a single person, alone.

clue.text: Go up higher in short descant arrangement

indicators.note: something short is lacking its end, so the final letter of the next word is dropped
an arrangement in music reworks material, so the letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written; a descant is a counter-melody sung above the tune

explanation.surface: A singer's voice rises higher in a descant arrangement of a hymn.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascend is to climb or rise to a higher position.

clue.text: Stays above water, till supplies appearing

blocks.note: first meaning: is buoyant on the surface
second meaning: sums of small change put in a cash register at the start of trading

explanation.walkthrough: 'till' looks like 'until' but is the cash register; a float is the change it starts the day with.
explanation.definitionFit: Something buoyant floats, and a shop's floats are the small cash reserves kept in its registers.

clue.text: In our sad arrangement, one unable to adapt?

indicators.note: an arrangement sets things out in a new order, so the preceding letters are reordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, part of the same fodder

explanation.surface: In our gloomy set-up, someone cannot cope with change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link word but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Figuratively a dinosaur is an old-fashioned person or thing that has failed to keep up with change, like the extinct reptiles.

clue.text: Only a lake

blocks.note: first meaning: nothing more than
second meaning: a pond or lake, chiefly in English place names

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as 'just a lake'; Windermere's name ends in this old word for a lake.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means no more than, and the noun is a poetic or dialect word for a stretch of standing water.

clue.text: Huge reduction in solid fuel

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it, wrapped by the outer word

blocks.note: coal is a solid fuel
a loss is a reduction

explanation.surface: A massive cut has been made in supplies of solid fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Colossal means enormous, from the Colossus, a gigantic statue.

clue.text: Half of medicals returned the same

indicators.note: taking half of a word keeps only part of it, here its front four letters
something returned goes back the way it came, so the letters are read right to left

blocks.note: taken as written; its eight letters split into two halves

explanation.surface: Half the medical examinations came back with identical results.
explanation.walkthrough: IDEM is Latin, used in references to mean the same author or source as just cited.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word is used in footnotes to point back to the same author or work just cited.

clue.text: Some pest, rodent, made determined progress

indicators.note: some of a phrase is just a part of it, so the answer is a run of letters within those words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A pest, a rat perhaps, scuttled purposefully forward.
explanation.definitionFit: To stride is to walk with long, decisive steps, and the past tense describes purposeful forward movement.

clue.text: Make amends together

blocks.note: first meaning: to make up for a wrong
second meaning: read as two words, '...', in harmony

explanation.walkthrough: The verb historically comes from being 'at one' with someone, so split into two words it means united.
explanation.definitionFit: Atoning repairs a wrong; 'at one' describes people who are in agreement or united.

clue.text: Almond fanatic?

blocks.note: first meaning: an almond is an example of an edible kernel in a shell
second meaning: an informal word for an enthusiast, as in a health freak

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone obsessed with almonds; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: An almond is one kind of nut, and informally a nut is an obsessive enthusiast.

clue.text: Given third class ranking, and boxed

blocks.note: C is the third grade after A and B
being ranked is being rated

explanation.surface: Something rated third class has been packed into a box.
explanation.definitionFit: To crate goods is to pack them in a wooden box for transport.

clue.text: Hot left back in charge of a learner

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: port is the left side of a ship
i/c is the abbreviation for in charge
taken as written
L is the learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A sweaty left back is captaining a beginner on the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left back' looks like a football position, but it is left read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The tropics are the hottest regions of the earth, so tropical weather is hot and humid.

clue.text: Still so rubbish inside

indicators.note: inside places one part within the other, so the second word sits within the first

blocks.note: sic is Latin for thus or so, used to flag a quotation as printed
tat is cheap, tasteless junk

explanation.surface: It still looks like rubbish is inside, as it were.
explanation.definitionFit: Static means not moving, so it is a synonym of the adjective meaning motionless.

clue.text: Be caught within one mile: fool!

indicators.note: within means held inside, so the first pair of words goes inside another part

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written
taken as written
c is cricket shorthand for caught

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry at someone who gets caught a mile away.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface treats 'Be caught' as a passive verb, but the two words are separate pieces, and the mile is opened up after its first letter to take them.
explanation.definitionFit: An imbecile is a stupid person, a synonym for a fool or idiot.

clue.text: Skilful King of France takes time after promotion

indicators.note: after places what precedes it second, so the monarch and time follow the publicity piece

blocks.note: an ad is an advertisement, promotion of a product
roi is French for king
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A clever French monarch bides his time after being elevated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'promotion' suggests rising in rank, but here it is publicity.
explanation.definitionFit: Adroit means clever or dexterous with the hands or mind, so it is a synonym of skilful.

clue.text: Cut the grass three times

indicators.note: something cut is trimmed, so the next word loses its final letter

blocks.note: taken as written
rice is a cereal grass

explanation.surface: An instruction to mow the lawn three times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut the grass' reads as mowing, but Cut acts only on 'the'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrice is an old-fashioned word for on three occasions.

clue.text: Copy in Home Counties writer

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the first word goes within the area named

blocks.note: the Home Counties around London are in the South East of England, abbreviated SE
to crib is to copy someone else's work

explanation.surface: A writer in the Home Counties is producing copy.
explanation.definitionFit: A scribe was a person who wrote out documents by hand; it is also a jocular word for a journalist.

clue.text: Destroys gains

blocks.note: first meaning: ruins or damages, a verb
second meaning: plunder or loot, a plural noun

explanation.walkthrough: The verb and the noun are unrelated meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: To spoil something is to ruin it, and the spoils of war are the booty or profits won.

clue.text: Dance on one leg?

blocks.note: first meaning: an informal social dance
second meaning: to jump on a single foot

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the second meaning is described rather than defined: moving on one leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A hop is an informal dance party, and hopping is springing along on one foot.

clue.text: Someone having a go in German city

blocks.note: first meaning: a person who makes an attempt
second meaning: an ancient city on the Moselle in western Germany

explanation.walkthrough: Trier, near the Luxembourg border, is often claimed as Germany's oldest city.
explanation.definitionFit: A trier is one who tries or attempts, and Trier is a city in the Rhineland.

clue.text: In poverty, recession, one affected by inflation

indicators.note: in means lying within, so the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows

blocks.note: the letters straddle the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone in poverty during a recession is hit hard by rising prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inflation' suggests economics in this scene of hardship, but it means pumping up with air.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyre is inflated with air, so it is something literally affected by inflation.

clue.text: Workplace not on rocks

blocks.note: off is the opposite of on
a drink on the rocks is served with ice

explanation.surface: A workplace that is not heading for disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: An office is a room or building where clerical or professional work is done.

clue.text: Fruit in fridges, oddly

indicators.note: oddly points at the odd-numbered positions, first, third and so on, keeping only those

blocks.note: letters one, three, five and seven of the word

explanation.surface: Fruit is kept in fridges, strangely.
explanation.definitionFit: Figs are the soft, sweet fruit of the fig tree, so they are an example of fruit.

clue.text: Performance of Callas, perhaps: missing the start

indicators.note: something missing its start has lost its opening, so the first letter is dropped

blocks.note: Maria Callas was a famous opera soprano; 'perhaps' marks her as one example of someone so named

explanation.surface: A rendition by the diva Callas that leaves out the opening.
explanation.walkthrough: Callas wants to be the singer of the piece, but she supplies only her first name.
explanation.definitionFit: An aria is a solo song in an opera, the sort of piece a soprano performs.

clue.text: Moving close to you, a Gallic despot

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept
moving things shifts them about, so the letters are put in a fresh order

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Frenchman edges closer to you and turns out to be a tyrant.
explanation.definitionFit: Caligula was a Roman emperor notorious for cruelty and tyranny, an example of a despot.
